div.p: In this paper, we propose an O(v 2 ) scalable duplication based algorithm (RT-SDA) for scheduling precedence constrained real-time tasks on heterogeneous multiprocessors. This models a network of workstations, with processors of varying computing power. The algorithm takes the heterogeneities of both computation and communication of the multiprocessor system into account. RT-SDA employs selective task duplication to reduce the start time of the real-time tasks in the job, thereby increasing the guarantee ratio of the real-time application. Moreover, our scheme is scalable in that the application can be scheduled even if the available number of processors is less than the required number of processors. Compared to the existing scheduling algorithms in the literature, RT-SDA offers better schedulability in terms of a higher guarantee ratio.

div.head: Introduction and Related Work
div.p: In a real-time computer system, the timeliness of the availability of results is also a constraint in addition to their correctness. Some examples of real-time systems are real time database systems, process control systems, flight control systems, and web browsers (audio and video). As current real-time systems become more and more complex, there is an increasing need for them to be implemented on multiple (rather than single) heterogeneous processor platforms. Such a system would consist of multiple modules with different speeds and configurations that communicate with each other to execute a given task. These modules may be connected with variable bandwidth links. Examples of such systems are image processing, weather modeling, and fluid flow systems.

Real time scheduling on a uniprocessor has been an extensively studied problem in the literature [1][2][3][4][5][6][7]. One of the seminal works in real time scheduling has been carried out in [1]. The paper proposes two algorithms for scheduling periodic tasks on a single processor -the rate monotonic (RM) algorithm and the earliest deadline first (EDF) algorithm. The schedulability of a periodic task set on a uniprocessor has been proved to be an NP-hard problem [2].

Harbour et al. [3] present a timing analysis for a hard realtime periodic task set using a fixed priority-scheduling algorithm. The scheduling of aperiodic tasks on hard realtime systems has been proposed in [6]. All of this research [1-7] assumes that the real-time system comprises of a single processor. Hence, they cannot be directly implemented on a multiprocessor platform.

Papers [8][9][10][11][12][13] address the scheduling of real-time tasks on homogeneous multiprocessors. Abdelzaher and Shin [8] present an algorithm for the offline scheduling of communicating periodic tasks with precedence and exclusion constraints. In [9], Kaneko et al. propose an integrated scheduling scheme capable of handling both hard and soft real-time applications. Manimaran and Siva Ram Murthy [11] discuss an algorithm for the non-preemptive scheduling of aperiodic real-time tasks on a set of multiprocessors. Chetto et al. [12] deal with the pipelined scheduling of periodic tasks in distributed real-time systems. However, all these papers [8][9][10][11][12][13] assume that the processor platform is homogeneous. Hence, these scheme are not suitable for heterogeneous systems.

In comparison, the area of real-time scheduling on heterogeneous multiprocessors has received considerably little attention [14-17, 24, 27]. Recent papers [14,15] extend the popular EDF algorithm for a set of heterogeneous multiprocessors. One of the limitations of this work is that it assumes independence between the periodic tasks. In general, there is always some kind of precedence relationship between tasks such that a task can start only after it has received the results from all of its predecessors. Qin et al. investigate an offline-scheduling algorithm for precedence constrained real-time tasks in a heterogeneous environment [17]. Ramamritham proposes a scheme to schedule precedence related homogeneous periodic tasks by clustering heavily communicating tasks together and then mapping them on to the system processors [18]. But if the number of available processors is less than the initial set of clusters, the real-time application becomes unschedulable. In our proposed scheme, such a condition is addressed by assigning extra clusters to dummy processors, which are then merged with the available processors.

Task duplication has been employed previously in the literature for providing fault-tolerance in the schedule [17,[19][20][21][22][23]. Qin et al [17] use a primary backup (PB) approach to deal with a single processor failure. Our aim in employing task duplication is to increase the guarantee ratio of the realtime application. In our previous work [24], we had proposed a reliability driven real time scheduling algorithm for heterogeneous systems. The roots of our algorithm can be found in [25]. An optimal algorithm for scheduling a set of precedence related tasks on a heterogeneous system has been discussed in [26]. In [27], the authors develop a number of heuristics to schedule precedence constrained real-time tasks on a set of heterogeneous multiprocessors.

In this research, we propose a Real-Time Scalable Duplication based Algorithm (RT-SDA) that employs selective task duplication to increase the guarantee ratio of real-time applications. Our algorithm is based on computing some mathematical quantities. In the first step, an initial set of clusters is generated and each cluster is assigned to a different processor. If the number of available processors is greater than the initial number of generated clusters, task duplication is carried out. Otherwise, the extra clusters are merged on to the clusters that are already allotted to processors. This procedure is invoked till the number of clusters is equal to the number of available processors.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the system model and the mathematical quantities used by the algorithm. Section 3 explains the working principles of the proposed algorithm along with its pseudocode. A running example is presented in section 4. Section 5 discusses the simulation results and finally, section 6 concludes the paper.

div.head: System Model
div.p: A real-time job executing on the system is represented by a real-time directed acyclic graph RTDAG = (N, E, P, C, c). N = {n 1 , n 2 , n 3 ,…, n x } stands for the set of task nodes and each node represents a real-time task. The set of communication edges is denoted by the set E, where E = {e 1 , e 2 , e 3 , … , e q } and P = {p 1 , p 2 , p 3 , … , p m } represents the set of heterogeneous processors. C(n i ,p k ) is the execution time of task n i on processor p k , where n i ∈N and p k ∈P. The communication cost between two tasks is given by c(n i ,n j ), where n i ,n j ∈ N and i≠j. The deadline of a real-time job is denoted by d. The set of predecessors of a task n i ∈N is given by Pred(n i ). Similarly, Succ(n i ) denotes the set of successor tasks for n i . AP denotes the available number of processors. The critical number of processors required for the initial cluster generation is denoted by CNP.

A task is assumed to be non-preemptive and indivisible. We assume that the processors are dedicated, i.e., they are free unless a task has been scheduled to execute on them. A fully connected network with dedicated communication channels has been assumed. This means that any number of messages can pass through the channels without any restriction.

div.head: An overview of RT-SDA
div.p: The set of real-time tasks (N) and the set of heterogeneous multiprocessors (P) are fed to the algorithm as input. The pseudocode of RT-SDA is given in Figure 1. In the first step, the est, ect, fpred, fp and level values are calculated for each real-time task in the RTDAG in a topbottom traversal. The level of a task is defined as the highest summation of computation costs along different paths to the exit node from the node under consideration. The next step involves a bottom-up traversal of the RTDAG to calculate last and lact. A data structure called the queue is then formed. It consists of all the real-time tasks arranged in a non-decreasing order of level. Then, each real-time task in the RTDAG is checked for feasibility. Specifically, if the sum of the est of a task and its worst case execution time is greater than the deadline, the task schedule is not feasible. All the feasible tasks are moved to queue and all the non-feasible tasks are inserted into another data structure called, queue1. The elements of queue1 are then sorted in a non-decreasing order of their average execution costs. In the next stage, the initial cluster generation takes place. The algorithm for this stage is given in Figure 2. Here, an initial set of clusters is generated using available processors. The RTDAG is traversed bottom-up starting with the exit node. The aim is to try to generate clusters by following the favorite predecessor chain till the entry node is reached. If the fpred has already been assigned or if it is not critical, an unassigned predecessor having the lowest execution time on the current processor is selected. The significance of task criticality (definition 7) is that if two tasks are not critical to each other, they can be assigned to different processors. Once a cluster is formed, the next cluster is built starting with the next unassigned element of the queue. This process continues recursively, till all the queue elements have been exhausted. Each cluster is then assigned to the first available fp of the header task of that cluster. For example, if fp1 has already been assigned to another cluster, then fp2 is chosen to accommodate the cluster. If fp2 has also been assigned, then fp3 is chosen and so on.

If the number of available processors (AP) is greater than the number of processors required by the initial set of clusters (CNP), task duplication is carried out to increase the guarantee ratio of the real-time application. A check is carried out to see if each task in a cluster is preceded by its fpred task. If this is not the case, then the tail of that particular cluster is replaced with its fpred chain till the entry node. The cut off tail is assigned to the next available fp of the last node of that tail. Duplication is carried out till all tasks are preceded by their fpred tasks or till there are no more processors remaining. After the duplication stage, a check is carried to see if there are more slots available to insert one (or more) elements of queue1 (since duplication reduces the completion time of the application, the tasks that were earlier not feasible can now be inserted in the schedule). The selected tasks are then inserted in the schedule and the guarantee ratio is calculated.

The execution time of a real-time task on a dummy processor is the average run time of that task. The clusters are then arranged in a non-increasing order of exec(p k ), where exec(p k ) is defined to be the sum of execution costs of all the tasks assigned to p k ∈P. Then the least populated cluster of a real processor is merged with the most populated cluster of a dummy processor. This process is carried out till the number of clusters becomes equal to the number of processors. The level of a task is used to find out the place where the task is to be inserted. The tasks are inserted so that the non-decreasing level value is maintained as we go from a large number task to a small number task.

div.head: A Running Trace of RT-SDA
div.p: In this section, we shall illustrate the working of RT-SDA with the help of an illustrative example. Consider the RTDAG shown in Figure 4. The run times of real-time tasks on the system processors are given in Table 2. The deadline has been selected to be 45. The values obtained after invoking steps 2, 3 and 4 of Figure 1 are tabulated in Table 1. The elements of the queue are {12, 11, 10, 9, 6 7, 8, 5, 3, 4, 2, 1}. The generation of the first cluster starts from 12. It is preceded by its fpred, which is 9. Task 9 is preceded by its fpred, task 5. Continuing in a similar fashion, the next tasks will be 2 and 1.

Hence, the first cluster is 12-9-5-2-1. This is assigned to the fp 1 of task 12, which is P 5 . The next cluster starts from the next unassigned element of queue, which happens to be 11. The next element in this cluster will be the fpred of 11, which is 7. The fpred of 7 is 3 but it has already been assigned to the first cluster. So task 4 is chosen as the next task. The final task is 1. So, the second cluster is 11-7-4-1.This is assigned to the fp 1 of 11, which is P 1 . In a similar manner, the third cluster is 10-6-3-1. It is assigned to P 2 . The final cluster is 8-4-1 and this is assigned to P 7 . The complete schedule is shown in Figure 5. It has a schedule length of 34 time units.

Cluster 1, which is the least populated cluster to own a real processor accommodates cluster 3, which is the most populated processor to own a dummy processor. It has a schedule length of 41 time units. Theorem 1. Let v be number of vertices, p be the number of heterogeneous processors, and e be the number of communication edges in the RTDAG. Then the worst case complexity of RT-SDA is given by O(V 2 ).

Proof. The complexity of the first stage (est, ect, fpred, fp, level, queue) is O(v(p+p*log 2 p)), where p is the number of processors and v is the number of nodes. For most practical DAGs, v>>p and v is of the order of plog 2 p. Hence, the average complexity is O(v 2 ). The second step (last and lact) is a bottom-up traversal and its complexity is O(e). The complexity of the formation of the queue is vlog 2 v. The next step (checking tasks for feasibility and adding infeasible tasks to queue1) has complexity O(2v+log 2 v). The third step is similar to depth first search (cluster generation) and its complexity is O(v+e). For a connected graph, it is O(e) in the worst case. In the duplication stage, the complexity is O(tv) where t is the number of tasks not using fpred . In the worst case, t=v. So, the complexity becomes O(v 2 ).The compaction stage involves sorting the processors based on empty slots. Therefore, each pass though the compaction code is of the order of O(v+p*log 2 p) with p=v in the worst case scenario. The number of required passes depends on the difference between AP and RP and is given by Q=log 2 (RP/AP).In the worst case, RP=v and AP=1. So, Q=log 2 (v). Therefore, the complexity of compaction is O(v 2 ). The complexity of inserting previously infeasible elements is O(v). Hence, the overall complexity = O(v(p+plog 2 p)+2v+log2v+e +vlog 2 v+v+e+v+v 2 ). For most practical applications, the first term can be substituted as v 2 as v>>p and v=plog 2 p. Therefore, the complexity of RT-SDA is O(v 2 ).

div.head: Experimental Results
div.p: In this section, we shall discuss our simulation results. Input graphs that realistically model real-time applications have been generated randomly. Random graphs have been widely used by researchers in the past to test the performance of their scheduling algorithms [17,24,27]. In addition, real-time application programs presented in [28,29] have also been tested. Three performance metrics have been used to evaluate the proposed scheme. The first measure is the Guarantee Ratio (GR), which is the number of tasks that meet their deadlines to the total number of tasks in the set. The second measure, called Scalability Factor (SF), is the ratio of available processors (AP) and critical number of processors (CNP). The third metric called the heterogeneous factor (HF) is defined as average {((max. task cost -min. task cost)/2) / average task cost}. The total communication to total computation ratio (CCR) is defined as (total edge cost/ (total node cost).

div.head: Workload
div.p: The task execution times have been uniformly selected from the range [min_e, max_e]. The volume of data to be transmitted between the real-time tasks has been randomly generated so that the CCR value is in the range [0, 10]. A single deadline is associated with a real-time job. Such a deadline is referred to as a common deadline or an end-toend deadline [17,27]. Specifically, the deadline of a task set is given by d = Ω (rt-dag) + α, where Ω (rt-dag) is the critical path length of the RTDAG and α is a constant parameter selected uniformly from a specified range [min α, max α].

div.head: Comparison of RTPSA with AEAP
div.p: In this set of experiments, we compare the performance of our scheme RT-SDA with two other schemes from the literature, namely RTPSA [24] and AEAP [27].The task execution time has been selected uniformly from the range the curves is the average of data obtained from 25 runs of the algorithms. The results for CCR=0.1 are depicted in Figure 9. We observe from the Figure that RT-SDA outperforms both RTPSA and AEAP in terms of GR. The reason is that RT-SDA employs selected task duplication to cut down the inter processor communication between processors. This leads to more tasks completing before the deadline. Hence, the GR value of the application increases. The GR value of RT-SDA is 11.2% on average and 21% at best larger than AEAP. On the other hand, the GR value of RT-SDA is 8% on average and 17% at best larger than RTPSA. For CCR=1.0 (Figure 10), the results are again Figure 10. GR vs. N for CCR=1.0 quite significantly in favor of RT-SDA. Specifically, the GR of RT-SDA is 16.8% on average and 27% at best larger than AEAP. Also, the GR of RT-SDA is 13% on average and 20% at best larger than RTPSA.

The results for CCR=10.0 are shown in Figure 11. This time, the GR of RT-SDA is 17% on average and 31% at best larger than AEAP. Moreover, RT-SDA outperforms RTPSA by 14% on average and 27 % at best in terms of the GR value. From the above study, we observe that the improvement in GR is more significant for CCR values of 1.0 and 10.0 than for a CCR of 0.1. div.head: Results for application graphs
div.p: To validate our scheduling algorithm, we also performed experiments on two real-time application programs presented in [28,29]. The first application consisted of a graph of 18 tasks and the second application consisted of a graph of 50 tasks. In the above papers [28,29], all the processors were assumed to be identical and the communication costs were assumed to be negligible. The results are shown in Figure 12. From the figure, we observe that the performance of all the tested algorithms is more or less the same. Considering that we had to downgrade RT-SDA for this comparison, we can conclude that RT-SDA is more powerful because it can schedule tasks with precedence constraints on heterogeneous multiprocessors.

div.head: Effect of Scalability Factor
div.p: In the first experiment, the relationship between the scalability factor (SF) of a real-time application and its GR has been studied. The scalability factor is a measure of the degree of scalability in the heterogeneous system. This experiment has been conducted for graphs of size 120, 140, 160, 180 and 200. The results are shown in Figure 13. From the figure, we observe that in general, guarantee ratio increases with an increase in the scalability factor. That is because as the value of SF increases, the difference between AP and CNP reduces. Specifically, when SF is greater than 1, the extra processors available to the system are employed for duplication. This leads to real-time tasks finding earlier start times. Consequently, more tasks meet their deadline and the GR value experiences an increase as well. A CCR value of 1.0 and an HF value of 1.0 have been assumed for this experiment.

In the second experiment, we have tried to capture the tradeoff between the scalability factor of a real-time application and its guarantee ratio. If the degree of scalability of a system is high, then the GR would be low and vice versa. The results of this study are shown in Table 4. We observe that as the SF value reduces, cluster compaction is carried out and the number of available processors reduces. Hence, the real-time tasks are assigned later start times and consequently, the GR experiences a decrement. However, this degradation has been observed to be graceful in our studies. A CCR of 1.0 has been assumed in this set of experiments.

div.head: Effect of Heterogeneity Factor
div.p: This experiment evaluates the effect of the heterogeneity factor (HF) of a real-time application as a function of its guarantee ratio (GR).The value of min_e has been kept fixed at 20 and max_e value has been incremented by a constant factor of 4. The results are depicted in Figure 14. We observe that as the HF value of the system increases, there is more variation in the execution times of the real- time tasks. Since the deadline of a real-time task has been assumed to be a function of its execution time, this leads to a looser deadline. Hence the GR value of the task set increases. A CCR value of 1.0 has been assumed.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, we have presented a scalable real-time scheduling algorithm called RT-SDA for heterogeneous multiprocessor systems. Selective task duplication has been employed to increase the guarantee ratio of the real-time application. Our algorithm needs a minimum number of processors to accommodate the initial set of clusters. If the system has more processors than this critical number, then task duplication is carried out, otherwise cluster compaction is done. To assess the performance of RT-SDA, it was compared with RTPSA and AEAP. The simulation results point to significant gains in guarantee ratios when an adequate number of processors are available. We also note that compaction results in a decrease in the task guarantee ratio. However, this degradation has been observed to be graceful. As a follow up to this work, we plan to propose an analytical test for determining whether a given periodic task set will be feasibly scheduled upon such a heterogeneous multiprocessor platform.
